channel.title: Federal Election Interference Risk Map
channel.description: Tracking DOJ lawsuits, FBI actions, and Project 2025 implementation across all 50 US states ahead of the 2026 midterms.

item.title: NAACP sues DOJ for records on its plan to send about 1,000 monitors to the polls
item.description: On October 2 the NAACP sued the Justice Department in federal court under the Freedom of Information Act after its September 1 request went unanswered. The suit seeks the legal authority for DOJ's plan to deploy about 1,000 federal personnel to polling places in November, the monitors' training and planned locations, and whether the FBI, ICE, or DHS will take part.

item.title: Supreme Court lets DHS resume expanded SAVE citizenship checks; Ohio, Georgia, and New Hampshire moves
item.description: On September 25 the Supreme Court, 6-3, paused Judge Sparkle Sooknanan's ruling that the overhauled SAVE citizenship database violates federal privacy law, the Social Security Act, and the Administrative Procedure Act, letting states again run bulk checks of their voter rolls against it through November; Justices Jackson, Sotomayor, and Kagan dissented. The same day, Judge Paula Xinis ordered the government to give her court 30 days' notice before releasing the state citizenship lists called for by Trump's March executive order, making October 28 the earliest possible release. On September 24 a divided 6th Circuit panel let Ohio require documentary proof of citizenship to register at the BMV. On September 28 Georgia's State Election Board voted 3-2 to ask DOJ and DHS to press the Secretary of State to change the state's QR-code ballot system before November. On October 2 a federal judge declined to block New Hampshire's ban on student IDs as voter identification for the general election.

item.title: DOJ falls to 0 for 26 as Vermont, Washington, and Georgia voter-data suits are dismissed
item.description: Three more federal judges dismissed the Justice Department's suits for states' unredacted voter rolls in September: Vermont (September 17), Washington (September 22, with prejudice), and Georgia (September 30). In Georgia, Judge Victoria Calvert ruled that federal law does not override the state's voter-privacy law and that the Civil Rights Act does not entitle DOJ to the full roll; it was DOJ's second Georgia suit after the first was dismissed in January for being filed in the wrong court. DOJ has now lost all 26 district-court rulings on the merits. The 6th Circuit affirmed Michigan's dismissal and denied rehearing; appeals of other dismissals are pending in 10 federal circuits. Oklahoma settled and handed over its data. Cases in Delaware, Utah, Hawaii, and Idaho remain undecided. No court at any level has ruled for DOJ.

item.title: Judge strikes election conditions from DHS anti-terrorism grants
item.description: On September 28, Judge Amir Ali of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia vacated FEMA's requirement that states and localities check voter rolls against DHS's SAVE citizenship database, hand-audit 5 percent of ballots, and move to hand-marked ballots or lose 20 percent of their Homeland Security Grant Program funds. He held that Congress never authorized FEMA to use counterterrorism grants to force changes in how elections are run. The suit was brought by six counties and cities, including Harris and El Paso counties in Texas, Nashville, and Columbus. A separate suit by 23 states is still pending, and DHS says it will impose new requirements.

item.title: Supreme Court orders Missouri to use its 2022 congressional map in November
item.description: In a unanimous unsigned order on September 25, the Supreme Court held that "the 2022 map — not the 2025 map — must be used in the 2026 congressional election." The order ended a month of conflicting rulings: the Missouri Supreme Court held on September 3 that the 2025 map never took effect because of a citizen referendum against it; a federal judge on September 8 and the 8th Circuit on September 21 ordered the 2025 map instead; and on September 10 the Missouri Supreme Court found Secretary of State Denny Hoskins in contempt for following the federal order, which he reversed the same day. Absentee voting had already begun. Voters will decide the 2025 map as Proposition A on November 3.

item.title: Texas: 200,000 voter registrations stalled; Tarrant County cuts 92 polling sites
item.description: The Texas Department of Public Safety failed to send counties at least 200,000 voter registration applications and updates submitted through its online driver's-license portal since October 2025, which DPS blamed on a third-party vendor's software update. The state says affected voters who do not appear on the rolls can cast a provisional ballot that will count once their registration is confirmed. Separately, on September 1 Tarrant County commissioners voted 3-2 along party lines to cut Election Day polling sites from 316 in the 2022 midterms to 224 this November, in a county of more than 1.3 million registered voters.

item.title: California expands its state Voting Rights Act
item.description: Governor Gavin Newsom signed SB 1164 and SB 1360 on September 19. The laws bar voter suppression and vote dilution, add a process to stop discriminatory voting changes before they take effect, and expand language access for voters with limited English. According to the NAACP Legal Defense Fund, California is the fourth state in 2026 to enact or expand a state Voting Rights Act, after Maryland, New Jersey, and Delaware.

item.title: Lawsuits seek to keep armed federal agents away from polling places
item.description: The NAACP, four national unions, and civil rights groups sued in federal court in Washington, D.C., on September 18 under the Voting Rights Act's ban on voter intimidation, asking the court to block deployment of federal agents to polling places. A September 10 suit by Denver Clerk Paul Lopez and a coalition including LULAC cites a Civil War-era federal law that makes it a crime to send armed federal officers to the polls. DHS says ICE is not planning operations targeting polling locations but that it may still make targeted arrests.

item.title: Supreme Court keeps the USPS mail-ballot rule blocked for the midterms
item.description: On September 14 the Supreme Court denied the Justice Department's emergency request to let the Postal Service enforce its new mail-ballot rule, finding the government "unlikely to succeed on the merits" of its challenge to Judge Indira Talwani's September 4 preliminary injunction. Justices Alito and Thomas dissented; Justice Kavanaugh concurred, writing that applying the rule in 2026 would be arbitrary and capricious because election officials lack time to implement it. The rule would have required pre-approved ballot-envelope designs, a unique barcode for each voter, and states uploading voter rosters to a USPS portal. On September 13 a second judge, Carl Nichols in Washington, D.C., separately blocked the rule, writing that "No statute grants the Postal Service the power to issue key parts of the Rule," and on September 10 the 1st Circuit refused to lift Talwani's injunction.

item.title: DOJ warns 29 states and D.C. of criminal sanctions over 2024 election records
item.description: Letters from Eric Neff, acting chief of the Justice Department's Voting Section, made public September 10, ordered the 29 states and the District of Columbia that DOJ is suing for voter data to preserve their 2024 election records, warning that failure "may constitute spoliation of evidence" that could bring "civil and criminal sanctions." Utah's Republican Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson said DOJ should "focus on actual problems instead of baselessly harassing election officials." In Wyoming, Republican Gov. Mark Gordon objected that two DOJ election monitors at the August 18 primary, who sought to examine tabulators and interview voters, behaved in a way that "seemed to exceed what the authority that Congress had given them was." DOJ plans to deploy about 1,000 monitors nationwide in November.

item.title: Maryland redistricting question restored to the ballot; Michigan citizenship amendment stays off
item.description: On September 3 the Supreme Court of Maryland overturned lower-court orders that had blocked Question 3, the congressional redistricting amendment, from the November ballot, but found the legislature's ballot wording misleading and replaced it with the purpose paragraph from the bill itself; Justice Steven Gould dissented, joined by Senior Justice Glenn Harrell. The same day, the U.S. Supreme Court and the Michigan Supreme Court rejected requests to put a citizenship-verification amendment on Michigan's ballot after the Board of State Canvassers deadlocked 2-2 on certifying it. That amendment would have required voters to prove citizenship to vote a full ballot, creating two separate voter rolls.

item.title: Mail-voting order blocked again after Supreme Court lifts one of two injunctions
item.description: The Supreme Court stayed Judge Talwani's June injunction 6-3 on August 24, holding only that she ruled before USPS finalized its rule and expressly declining to decide the order's legality. USPS published its final rule for federal ballot mail on August 21. Talwani lifted her own earlier nationwide order on August 26 in light of the Supreme Court's ruling, then issued a 14-day temporary restraining order against the finalized rule on August 27, finding the challengers likely to succeed and no evidence of mail-voting fraud in the record. Justice Jackson dissented from the August 24 order, writing that it "needlessly injects chaos and uncertainty into the upcoming midterm elections."

item.title: DOJ falls to 0 for 23 in voter-data campaign as 6th Circuit refuses rehearing
item.description: Five more district courts dismissed the Justice Department's voter-data suits after July 30: Illinois (July 31), Colorado (August 3), Washington, D.C. (August 6), Nevada (August 14), and Minnesota (August 17), bringing the merits total to 23 dismissals and zero wins. On August 14 the 6th Circuit denied DOJ's petition to rehear United States v. Benson en banc, leaving intact the only appellate ruling in the campaign. The 9th Circuit heard the California and Oregon appeals on May 19 and has not ruled.

item.title: DOJ hits 0 for 18 as New Jersey voter-data case is dismissed
item.description: Judge Zahid Quraishi dismissed the DOJ's lawsuit seeking New Jersey's voter registration database on July 29, ruling the Civil Rights Act does not authorize access — the administration's 18th consecutive district-court loss in the voter-data campaign, with zero wins. July also saw dismissals in New York, West Virginia, New Mexico, Virginia, Connecticut, and Kentucky, and the 6th Circuit affirmed Michigan's win on appeal. DOJ has appealed its losses to 8 federal circuits.

item.title: Trump asks Supreme Court to unleash mail-voting executive order before the midterms
item.description: After Judge Talwani blocked the core of the March 31 election EO for 2026 (June 25) and ruled Section 3 unconstitutional (July 23), and the 1st Circuit refused a stay (July 25), the administration filed an emergency application at the Supreme Court on July 27 seeking full implementation — USPS mail-ballot gatekeeping and the DHS/SSA citizenship database — before November 3. States' response is due August 3. The D.C. Circuit separately held a parallel challenge premature, splitting the circuits.

item.title: 23 states sue over DHS tying $1.5B in security grants to election mandates
item.description: An Illinois-led coalition of 23 states plus D.C. and the governors of Kentucky and Pennsylvania sued July 23 in the District of Rhode Island, challenging DHS's conditioning of Homeland Security Grant Program funds on hand-marked paper ballots, manual audits, and running voter rolls through the SAVE database — at least $148 million at stake. A week earlier, DHS Secretary Mullin conditioned CISA election-security help on SAVE screening and claimed, without methodology, that 250,000+ noncitizens are registered in CA, NJ, NV, and PA.

item.title: Trump's primetime election address; D.C. Guard extended through 2029
item.description: In a July 16 East Room address, Trump claimed China acquired 220 million voter files and that voter data in 18 states was "bought, stolen, or hacked," ordered the FBI to reopen the debunked Muskegon, Michigan registration case, and directed DHS to push states to purge rolls. Fact-checkers found no evidence for the central claims; prior state and federal probes of Muskegon found no fraudulent votes were cast. The same week, the White House confirmed the D.C. National Guard deployment — roughly 5,000 troops — will run through January 2029, spanning the midterms and the next presidential transition.

item.title: DOJ threatens election officials in all 50 states; monitors headed to 6 states; 260 FBI personnel on Georgia case
item.description: On July 7-8, Assistant AG Harmeet Dhillon sent letters warning election officials in all 50 states they could face criminal prosecution over noncitizens on voter rolls, with 5-day deadlines — Utah's Republican Lt. Gov. called the letter "truly bizarre... sprinkled throughout with threats of criminal prosecution." DOJ simultaneously announced federal election monitors for 15 jurisdictions in AZ, MA, MI, MN, NH, and VA. An internal FBI memo revealed 260 personnel assigned to the Fulton County case; a Trump-appointed judge quashed DOJ's subpoena for every Fulton election worker's identity as an "arbitrary fishing expedition." No state is known to have capitulated.

item.title: Supreme Court upholds mail-ballot grace periods in Watson v. RNC
item.description: In a 5-4 ruling on June 29 written by Justice Barrett, the Supreme Court held states may count mail ballots postmarked by Election Day but received afterward, upholding Mississippi's grace period. Postmark deadlines in 14+ states and military/overseas grace windows in roughly 30 survive intact for 2026 — the feared invalidation months before the midterms did not happen.

item.title: Callais guts VRA Section 2; Louisiana suspends an active election; Southern redistricting wave follows
item.description: The Supreme Court's April 29 Louisiana v. Callais ruling (6-3) struck Louisiana's second majority-Black district and held VRA compliance cannot justify race-conscious maps — Justice Kagan wrote that Section 2 is now "all but a dead letter." The next day, Gov. Landry suspended Louisiana's May 16 House primaries mid-election by executive order — the first gubernatorial suspension of an active congressional election in U.S. history — and the state later enacted a map eliminating Rep. Cleo Fields' majority-Black district. Tennessee split Memphis's majority-Black district in a 3-day special session; Florida enacted a map targeting four Democratic incumbents; the Supreme Court reinstated Alabama's blocked map 6-3 on the shadow docket. South Carolina's redraw failed in its state Senate.

item.title: Senate Republicans reject eliminating filibuster for SAVE Act
item.description: Senate Majority Leader John Thune firmly rejected proposals to eliminate the filibuster to pass the SAVE America Act, stating Republicans lack "anywhere close to the votes" for the nuclear option despite Trump pressure. Sen. Mike Lee pushed for a "talking filibuster" approach, but Thune expressed concerns about tying up the Senate floor for weeks.

item.title: West Virginia Secretary of State rejects DOJ voter data demands
item.description: West Virginia Secretary of State Kris Warner announced his office will not release personally identifying information of registered voters to the DOJ, stating that state law prohibits sharing unredacted voter information. Warner cited the recent Michigan court ruling dismissing DOJ's legal authority and said he would only provide publicly available, redacted voter lists.

item.title: Nebraska hands over voter data to DOJ after court loss
item.description: Nebraska Secretary of State Bob Evnen sent voter registration data including names, dates of birth, partial Social Security numbers, and addresses to the DOJ on February 12, 2026, after the Nebraska Supreme Court rejected a legal effort to block the transfer. Common Cause's lawsuit to prevent the data release was dismissed.

item.title: FBI invites all 50 state election officials to mysterious February 25 call
item.description: The FBI sent emails to election officials in all 50 states inviting them to a February 25 conference call to discuss 'preparations' for 2026 midterms. The email, signed by 'FBI Election Executive' Kellie Hardiman, provides no specific purpose and includes DOJ, DHS, USPIS, and EAC. Nevada Secretary of State called it 'beyond crazy' and asked 'Is this real?' Multiple officials said they had never seen the FBI organize such outreach before.

item.title: House passes SAVE America Act 218-213, first GOP senator opposes
item.description: The House voted 218-213 on Feb 11 to pass the SAVE America Act, an expanded version of the SAVE Act that requires proof of citizenship to register to vote, photo ID to cast a ballot, and monthly voter roll purges using DHS databases. All Republicans present voted yes; Rep. Henry Cuellar (D-TX) was the sole Democratic yes vote. Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-AK) became the first Republican senator to oppose, warning it federalizes elections — the same argument the GOP used against Democrats in 2021. The bill faces a 60-vote threshold in the Senate, where Majority Leader Thune says there are "not even close" to votes to eliminate the filibuster.

item.title: Nebraska court dismisses lawsuit blocking voter data transfer to DOJ
item.description: A Lancaster County judge dismissed Common Cause Nebraska's lawsuit attempting to block the transfer of voter data to the DOJ. The judge ruled on standing grounds, not the merits. Common Cause is appealing to the Nebraska Court of Appeals, but Secretary of State Evnen plans to proceed with the data transfer on Feb 12, 2026.

item.title: Trump-appointed judge dismisses Michigan voter data lawsuit
item.description: U.S. District Judge Hala Jarbou, a Trump appointee, dismissed the DOJ's lawsuit seeking Michigan's voter rolls. She ruled that none of the three federal laws cited — the Civil Rights Act of 1960, NVRA, and HAVA — require states to hand over the data. This is the third dismissal on the merits, after California and Oregon. The DOJ is now 0-for-3 in court.

item.title: Trump calls on Republicans to "nationalize the voting"
item.description: President Trump told conservative podcaster Dan Bongino that Republicans should "take over the voting in at least 15 places" and "nationalize the voting." The next day he doubled down, saying "I don't know why the federal government doesn't do them anyway." The Constitution explicitly delegates election administration to the states. Election experts called it an alarming escalation.

item.title: AG Bondi demands Minnesota voter rolls as condition for pulling ICE
item.description: Attorney General Pam Bondi sent a letter to Minnesota Governor Tim Walz demanding voter rolls and welfare data as conditions for withdrawing ICE from Minneapolis — hours after federal agents fatally shot a second person in the city. Minnesota Secretary of State Steve Simon called it "an apparent ransom to pay for our state's peace and security." Arizona's Secretary of State compared it to "organized crime."

item.title: Virginia becomes 24th state sued by DOJ for voter data
item.description: The Department of Justice has sued Virginia for voter registration data, making it the 24th state to face legal action over refusal to hand over sensitive voter information including Social Security numbers.

item.title: FBI raids Fulton County, Georgia election offices
item.description: The FBI raided Fulton County election offices on January 28, seizing 2020 ballots and voter rolls. DNI Tulsi Gabbard was on-site and reportedly called President Trump during the raid. This represents the first direct federal law enforcement action against state election infrastructure.

item.title: Federal judge dismisses Georgia voter data lawsuit on jurisdictional grounds
item.description: A federal judge dismissed the DOJ's voter data lawsuit against Georgia because the government filed in the wrong court (Macon instead of Atlanta). The case was dismissed without prejudice, meaning DOJ can refile. Unlike the California and Oregon dismissals, this was not a ruling on the merits of DOJ's legal theory.

item.title: Courts dismiss California and Oregon voter data cases
item.description: Federal courts dismissed the DOJ's voter data lawsuits against both California and Oregon. The California judge found "an alarming picture regarding the centralization of Americans' information within the Executive Branch."

item.title: DOJ files second wave of voter data lawsuits
item.description: The Department of Justice sued Wisconsin, Illinois, Georgia, Washington D.C., Delaware, Maryland, New Mexico, Rhode Island, Vermont, Washington state, and others in a second wave of lawsuits demanding voter registration data including sensitive personal information.

item.title: DOJ sues first wave of states for voter data
item.description: The Department of Justice sued California, Michigan, Minnesota, New Hampshire, New York, Oregon, and Pennsylvania for refusing to hand over complete voter registration files including driver's license numbers and partial Social Security numbers.

item.title: CISA gutted — 1,000+ election security staff lost
item.description: The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency has lost over 1,000 employees through firings, layoffs, and transfers. CISA had helped local election officials protect voting systems from hacking. Dismantling CISA was a key Project 2025 recommendation.
